title: A free-body and force diagram: which forces act?
summary: The body is drawn alone, with every force on it as an arrow from its point of application. Arrow length is proportional to the force with a stated scale, and colour names the kind of force. The diagram is the first step to Newton's second law.

media.alt: A small box on a 25 degree incline with four arrows from its centre: a long amber weight pointing down, a sky-blue normal force perpendicular to the slope, a short teal applied force up the slope and a short rose friction arrow along the slope. A scale bar labelled 10 N sits at the bottom right.
media.caption: Reference render of class F4.1 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data. Standard theory only.

read_the_figure.question: Which forces act?
read_the_figure.axes: No numeric axes. The incline (grey wedge, 25 degrees) is drawn to scale with the box on it. Each arrow starts at the box centre; its length is the force times 0.11 length units per newton, with a scale bar of 10 N bottom right. Colour: weight amber, normal sky blue, applied teal, friction rose.
look_at: List every arrow and say what exerts it: weight (Earth), normal (surface), applied (a push), friction (surface).
Compare arrow lengths with the 10 N scale bar to read each magnitude.
Do the forces add to zero? Sum along the slope and perpendicular to it.
Which arrow's direction would you question, and why?
as_drawn: Labels: weight mg = 20 N, normal N = 18.1 N, applied P = 5.0 N, friction f = 3.5 N, with a note 'static equilibrium'. The numbers are consistent: N = 20 cos 25 degrees = 18.13 and f = 20 sin 25 degrees - 5 = 3.45.

The friction arrow is drawn pointing DOWN the slope. For equilibrium it must point UP the slope: the weight pulls the box down the slope with 8.45 N, the push gives 5 N up, and friction must supply the remaining 3.45 N up. With the arrow as drawn the forces do not sum to zero (the resultant is 6.9 N). Always check a free-body diagram by summing the arrows.
Arrows are drawn from the box centre for all forces; the normal force would in reality be spread over the contact face.
read_the_figure.proves: That the listed forces are the ones the diagram's author believes act, and (if the arrows are right) that they balance. It does not prove the list is complete: a missing force is invisible.
if_wrong: Forces that do not sum to zero in a body claimed to be at rest: a direction or a magnitude is wrong.
Arrows with no scale: relative sizes are guesses.
A force drawn that the body exerts on something else: it does not belong in this body's diagram.
must_check: arrow length to scale or stated

terms.meaning: A sketch of one body isolated from its surroundings, with all external forces on it shown as arrows.
The push of a surface perpendicular to itself.
The force along a surface that resists sliding or its tendency.
No acceleration: the vector sum of the forces is zero.
The gravitational force on the body, m g, straight down.
Parts of a force along chosen axes, here along and perpendicular to the slope.

remember: Isolate the body; draw only forces ON it.
Arrow length proportional to the force with a stated scale; colour by kind.
Resolve along and perpendicular to the slope; sums must be zero at rest.
Friction opposes the tendency to slide and satisfies f <= mu N.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Each arrow is a vector mark from the point of application: its direction is the force's direction and its length is the size, at a constant scale (here 0.11 units per newton). Colour separates force types. A scale bar translates length into newtons; labels give the numbers.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Newton's second law is a statement about the sum of all forces on one body, so the right picture isolates the body and lists them. Drawing every force from one point turns a vector sum into something the eye can check: do the arrows close up? Resolving along and perpendicular to the slope turns two vector equations into simple scalar ones.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: A missing force or one in the wrong direction is easy to overlook. Arrows of unequal scale look consistent but give wrong ratios. The force a body exerts on the ground is not on this diagram. The normal force is shown as a single arrow although it is a distribution. And a labelled number that does not match the arrow length is a silent contradiction.

understand.title: Why each required item matters
understand.text: A stated arrow scale makes the lengths measurable; colour per type makes the legend unnecessary. The sum-to-zero check is not on the list but is the real test: this render shows why. The check discovers that the friction arrow has the wrong sense, even though its label (3.5 N) is right.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A force polygon (arrows placed tip to tail) shows equilibrium as a closed polygon. A table of components along and perpendicular to the slope gives the numbers. A friction-cone diagram shows the allowed directions of the contact force. For several bodies draw one diagram per body, with the interaction pairs on separate diagrams.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add the force polygon next to the diagram: the four arrows tip to tail should close. Add the friction cone: the angle arctan(mu) about the normal, with the resultant contact force inside it.

steps.title: Equilibrium along and perpendicular to the slope
steps.note: With m g = 20 N, theta = 25 degrees and P = 5 N: N = 18.13 N and f = 8.45 - 5 = 3.45 N, positive, so friction acts up the slope. Summing the drawn forces with f up gives (0, 0); with f down it gives a resultant of 6.9 N.

steps.title: Is the box really at rest?
steps.note: Friction needed is only 19 percent of the normal force, so any surface with a static coefficient of 0.19 or more holds the box.

worked.title: Reading the reference render
worked.problem: From the figure: (1) how many forces and what are they? (2) What do the labels give for the normal force and does it match 20 cos 25? (3) Do the arrows as drawn sum to zero?

solution.text: Four: weight (amber, 20 N), normal (blue, 18.1 N), applied (teal, 5.0 N) and friction (rose, 3.5 N).
N = 18.1 N matches mg cos 25 degrees = 20 x 0.9063.

Not as drawn: along the slope the weight gives 8.45 N down, the push 5 N up, so friction must be 3.45 N up the slope, but the rose arrow points down the slope. The numbers are right; the arrow direction is not.

worked.answer: Four forces; N = 18.1 N is consistent; the friction arrow should point up the slope for equilibrium, and the plot's arrow does not.

analyze.q: The label says friction is 3.5 N but the arrow points down the slope. Which is more likely wrong, and how do you decide?
If P were 10 N instead of 5 N, which way would friction act?
analyze.hint: Compare P with mg sin theta = 8.45.

analyze.q: Why do the weight and the normal force not form an action-reaction pair?

evaluate.q: A student's free-body diagram includes the force the block exerts on the ramp. What is wrong, and how would you check a diagram before calculating?
evaluate.hint: Only forces on the body; the sum test.

create: Draw the force polygon for this body and check that it closes.
Redraw the diagram with the friction arrow in the correct direction and with P = 10 N.

checks.q: What does a free-body diagram include and exclude?
checks.answer: It includes only forces acting on the isolated body. Forces the body exerts on others are excluded.

checks.q: A 20 N weight on a 25 degree slope: what is the normal force?
The arrows in a free-body diagram of a stationary body do not add to zero. List two causes.
checks.answer: A wrong arrow direction (as here for friction), a wrong magnitude, or a missing force such as a second support or a drag.
